study.title: Exodus 3 The burning bush, the call of Moses and the God who frees
study.overview: Exodus 3 shows God interrupting Moses' routine to reveal his holiness, his name, and his redeeming purpose. The chapter is not just an extraordinary spiritual experience: it is the preparation for the deliverance of Israel, with Moses being called to confront Pharaoh, to transmit the divine word to the elders, and to announce that God himself will act with power to take his people out of Egypt. The center of the chapter is God's initiative: he sees affliction, hears the cry, descends to deliver and commission his servant, while at the same time revealing something of his eternal identity.

outline.title: The manifestation of God in the bush
outline.explanation: Moses, caring for the flock in the desert, finds the unexpected sign of the burning bush that is not consumed. The text highlights the holiness of the place, the call by name and the reverent distance that must be before God. The revelation also places Moses before the God of the patriarchs, linking the present to the past of the covenant.

outline.title: God sees oppression and calls Moses to act
outline.explanation: The Lord declares that he saw the affliction of his people, heard his cry, and know his anguish. He announces that he went down to deliver them and commission Moses to speak to Pharaoh. Moses" objection to his own insufficiency receives the decisive answer: God's presence will accompany him.

outline.title: God's name and the message to Israel
outline.explanation: Moses asks how to answer if the people want to know the name of the God who sent him. God responds with his self-identification and sends Moses to gather the elders of Israel to announce that the Lord has visited them and will lead them from oppression to the promised land.

outline.title: The confrontation with Pharaoh and the exit with provision
outline.explanation: Moses must ask for a temporary exit to sacrifice to God, but the Lord already anticipates the resistance of the king of Egypt. Even so, it promises signs of judgment, deliverance by strong hand and favor among the Egyptians, culminating in the exit of the people with provision instead of empty.

study.context: The chapter is set when Moses is in the wilderness, caring for the flock of his father-in-law in Horeb. The text presents this hill as the scene of divine revelation, without requiring more historical data beyond the chapter itself. The narrative also connects God's present performance with the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, showing continuity between the ancient promise and the deliverance of Israel in Egypt.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God is holy, personal, and sovereign. He not only observes human pain; he sees it, hears it, and knows, and acts to redeem. His holiness demands reverence, as the order indicates not to approach and to take off the shoes. His identity is presented as eternal and not dependent on anything outside of himself, which sustains his ability to fulfill the promise. The vocation of Moses reveals that the work of God is advancing not by the self-confidence of the servant, but by the presence of the Lord Himself. There is also a strong theme of historical redemption: God frees an oppressed people, judges the oppressor, and makes his servants leave not as defeated fugitives, but as people led by God and supplied by him.

scholarViews.insight: The flame in the bush can represent the transcendent holiness of God, and the bush that is not consumed shows that God does not intend to destroy the instrument he uses for his purposes.
God notes the affliction of Israel and acts when it seemed too late; their intervention comes when the people and Moses had almost ceased to wait for deliverance.

The expression translated by Borrow is better understood as asking or requesting, not how to borrow in the modern sense; thus, the text describes the exit from Egypt with requests made to Egyptian women.

questions: What does God's holiness in Horeb correct in our way of dealing with daily worship, prayer and obedience?
In which areas do you, like Moses, tend to answer God's call by remembering more of your insufficiency than God's presence?
How does the promise that God sees, hears and knows the affliction of his people strengthens his faith in times of oppression or delay?
study.practice: Set aside time to recognize God's holiness before asking for anything from him. Then identify an area in which you feel incapable and make the same implicit prayer of the chapter: not trust in your own strength, but in the presence of God. If you are in a position of leadership or influence, commit to speaking clearly what God has revealed, without retaining the message for fear of rejection. Finally, practice concrete gratitude for God's provision, remembering that he not only calls for mission, but also sustains the way.
study.uncertainty: This study is limited to the chapter and the notes provided. No external data were used to broaden the historical, geographical or linguistic context. The readings of the commentators were treated as interpretations, and some notes mention broader theological connections that are not explicitly demonstrated by the chapter text.
